questions.stem: The Kharif cropping season in India corresponds to which period?

options.text: Sown with the onset of the southwest monsoon (June–July) and harvested in autumn (Sept–Oct)
Sown in winter (October–December) and harvested in spring (March–April)
Sown in summer (March–May) between the two main seasons

questions.explanation: Kharif (monsoon) crops are sown with the onset of the southwest monsoon (June–July) and harvested in September–October. Major Kharif crops: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, sugarcane, groundnut, soybean. Rabi crops (option B) are winter crops like wheat and gram. Zaid crops (option D) are short summer crops like watermelon and cucumber.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which Indian state is the largest producer of wheat?
questions.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is the largest wheat-producing state in India, owing to its vast Gangetic plain and extensive irrigation. Punjab and Haryana have higher productivity (yield per hectare) and are the backbone of the central pool procurement, but UP leads in total output. Madhya Pradesh has risen to become a major wheat producer too.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Green Revolution in India, which dramatically increased foodgrain production from the late 1960s, was most associated with which crop?
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution was most dramatically successful with WHEAT, especially in Punjab, Haryana, and western UP, using High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds (notably the dwarf varieties developed by Norman Borlaug). M. S. Swaminathan is called the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India'. Rice gains came later and were more uneven.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which type of soil is most ideal for cotton cultivation in India?
questions.explanation: Black soil (regur), found mainly in the Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh), is ideal for cotton — hence its nickname 'black cotton soil'. It is rich in lime, iron, magnesium and has high moisture-retention capacity. Alluvial soil is best for cereals; laterite for plantation crops; red soil for pulses and millets.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India is the world's largest producer of which of the following?
questions.explanation: India is the world's largest producer of milk (since 1998), a result of Operation Flood (the White Revolution) led by Verghese Kurien. India is also the largest producer of pulses, jute, and spices, and the second-largest producer of rice, wheat, sugarcane, and cotton. For wheat and rice, China is the largest producer.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which is the largest producer of rice in India?
questions.explanation: West Bengal is the largest rice-producing state in India, helped by its fertile Gangetic delta, high rainfall, and multiple cropping seasons (aus, aman, boro). Uttar Pradesh and Punjab are also major producers. Punjab has very high productivity and contributes heavily to central procurement, but West Bengal leads in total output.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 'White Revolution' in India refers to a dramatic increase in the production of:
questions.explanation: The White Revolution (Operation Flood, launched 1970) transformed India into the world's largest milk producer. Spearheaded by Verghese Kurien through the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) and the Amul cooperative model in Gujarat, it created a nationwide milk grid. Kurien is called the 'Father of the White Revolution' / 'Milkman of India'.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Match the 'revolution' with its product: which pairing is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Option C is INCORRECT. The Pink Revolution refers to MEAT and POULTRY processing (and sometimes onion/pharmaceuticals), NOT foodgrains. Correct pairings: Yellow = oilseeds, Blue = fisheries, Golden = horticulture/honey/fruits, Green = foodgrains, Silver = eggs/poultry, Round/Black = potato/petroleum. Foodgrains belong to the GREEN Revolution.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which crop is referred to as a 'plantation crop' and is grown extensively in the hilly regions of Assam and the Nilgiris?
questions.explanation: Tea is a major plantation crop grown on hill slopes of Assam (the largest tea-producing state), West Bengal (Darjeeling), and the Nilgiris in the south. Tea requires well-drained slopes, high rainfall, and a warm humid climate. Coffee is concentrated in Karnataka; rubber in Kerala; cardamom in the Western Ghats.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Minimum Support Price (MSP) for crops in India is recommended by which body?

options.text: Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)

questions.explanation: The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), under the Ministry of Agriculture, recommends MSP for various crops. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) takes the final decision. The Food Corporation of India (FCI) is the agency that actually procures grain at MSP for the central pool and PDS. CACP recommends MSP for ~23 crops.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which state is the largest producer of sugarcane in India?
questions.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is the largest sugarcane-producing state in India, concentrated in the fertile, well-irrigated Gangetic plains. Maharashtra is the second largest and often leads in sugar PRODUCTION (from sugarcane) due to higher recovery rates and cooperative sugar mills. UP leads in cane tonnage.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: 'Jhumming' is a term associated with which agricultural practice?
questions.explanation: Jhumming is the local name in northeastern India for shifting cultivation (slash-and-burn agriculture): a plot is cleared, burnt, cultivated for a few years, then abandoned for the soil to recover. It has different names across India — Podu (Andhra/Odisha), Bewar/Dahiya (MP), Kumari (Western Ghats). It is being discouraged due to deforestation and soil erosion.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which crop requires waterlogged conditions and high temperature, making the river deltas and coastal plains of India ideal for it?
questions.explanation: Rice (paddy) requires standing water (waterlogged fields), high temperature (>25°C), and high humidity, making river deltas (Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari, Kaveri) and coastal plains ideal. It needs ~100–200 cm of rainfall or assured irrigation. Wheat, bajra and gram are dry-season/less-water crops grown in different conditions.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The PM-KISAN scheme provides what kind of support to farmers?

options.text: Direct income support of ₹6,000 per year in three instalments

questions.explanation: PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi), launched in 2019, provides direct income support of ₹6,000 per year to eligible landholding farmer families, paid in three equal instalments of ₹2,000 via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). Crop insurance (option C) is provided separately under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which is the largest producer of coffee in India?
questions.explanation: Karnataka is by far the largest coffee-producing state in India (~70% of national output), concentrated in the districts of Kodagu (Coorg), Chikkamagaluru, and Hassan. India grows both Arabica and Robusta varieties. Kerala is the second largest producer. Indian coffee is largely shade-grown, valued in export markets.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a millet (coarse grain) promoted under India's 'Shree Anna' / International Year of Millets initiative?
questions.explanation: Ragi (finger millet) is a nutritious millet, along with jowar (sorghum) and bajra (pearl millet). India led the campaign for 2023 to be declared the International Year of Millets by the UN, and rebranded millets as 'Shree Anna'. Basmati and durum are rice/wheat varieties; arborio is a rice variety — none are millets.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which agency is responsible for procurement, storage, and distribution of foodgrains for the Public Distribution System (PDS) in India?
questions.explanation: The Food Corporation of India (FCI), established in 1965, procures foodgrains (mainly wheat and rice) at MSP, maintains buffer stocks, and distributes them for the PDS. NABARD is the apex rural development bank; APEDA promotes agri-exports; NAFED handles procurement of pulses/oilseeds and price stabilisation for horticultural produce.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which state is the largest producer of jute in India?
questions.explanation: West Bengal is the largest producer of jute in India, accounting for the majority of national output. Jute (the 'golden fibre') requires high temperature, heavy rainfall, and the alluvial soil of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta. India is the world's largest jute producer. Bihar and Assam are the next largest producers.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Leguminous crops like pulses are valuable in crop rotation primarily because they:

options.text: Require very little water to grow
Have the highest market price among all crops
Can be harvested mechanically with ease
Fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil through root nodules, improving soil fertility

questions.explanation: Leguminous crops (pulses such as gram, arhar, moong, urad) host nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) in their root nodules, converting atmospheric nitrogen into soil nitrogen. This naturally replenishes soil fertility, which is why pulses are rotated with cereals. India is the world's largest producer AND consumer of pulses.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which cropping season do crops like watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, and fodder crops grown between Rabi and Kharif belong to?
questions.explanation: The Zaid season is the short summer cropping season between the Rabi (winter) harvest and the Kharif (monsoon) sowing — roughly March to June. Zaid crops include watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, bitter gourd, and fodder crops. They depend on irrigation and warm dry weather. 'Aman' is a variety of rice grown in the Kharif season.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: A student is asked to identify the correct sequence of India's foodgrain self-sufficiency milestones. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: Green Revolution (mid-1960s, wheat) → buffer-stock build-up → India becomes a net foodgrain exporter in some years, despite remaining the largest pulses importer historically
India achieved foodgrain self-sufficiency before independence in 1947
The White Revolution preceded and caused the Green Revolution
India has always been a net exporter of all foodgrains since 1950

questions.explanation: The correct sequence: India faced severe food shortages and relied on PL-480 wheat imports from the US in the early 1960s; the Green Revolution (HYV wheat, from ~1966) transformed production; buffer stocks were built; and in good years India became a net foodgrain exporter. India was historically a large pulses importer (now improving). Options B and D are factually false; the White Revolution (dairy, 1970) came AFTER the Green Revolution.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The term 'Operation Greens', launched by the Government of India, was initially aimed at stabilising the supply and prices of which three commodities?
questions.explanation: Operation Greens, announced in the 2018-19 Budget, initially targeted the 'TOP' crops — Tomato, Onion, and Potato — to stabilise their supply chains and protect farmers from price volatility (modelled on Operation Flood for milk). It was later expanded to cover other fruits and vegetables ('TOP to TOTAL'). It is implemented by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which soil type, formed by the weathering of basaltic lava and intensely leached in high rainfall, is associated with tea, coffee, and cashew cultivation in India?
questions.explanation: Laterite soil forms under high temperature and heavy rainfall with intense leaching (silica washed out, leaving iron and aluminium oxides — giving the red colour). Found in the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, and parts of the northeast and Kerala, it suits plantation crops like tea, coffee, rubber, and cashew when manured. Cotton needs black soil; cereals need alluvial soil.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which revolution is correctly matched with the person who led it in India?

options.text: Green Revolution → M. S. Swaminathan; White Revolution → Verghese Kurien

questions.explanation: M. S. Swaminathan is the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India' (HYV wheat/rice). Verghese Kurien is the 'Father of the White Revolution' (Operation Flood, dairy, Amul). Options A and B swap the two leaders — a classic exam trap. The Blue Revolution (fisheries) is not attributed to a single famous individual in the way the Green and White revolutions are.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Why is the cultivation of sugarcane in Maharashtra and Karnataka often criticised on water-sustainability grounds despite high yields?

options.text: Sugarcane grows only in waterlogged delta soils unavailable there
Sugarcane depletes soil nitrogen faster than any other crop
Sugarcane is a long-duration, highly water-intensive crop, and growing it in drought-prone, irrigation-dependent Deccan regions diverts scarce water and stresses groundwater
Sugarcane cannot be processed locally, requiring costly transport

questions.explanation: Sugarcane is a long-duration (10–18 month) and extremely water-intensive crop. Large-scale cultivation in the drought-prone, rain-shadow Deccan regions of Maharashtra (e.g., Marathwada) and Karnataka relies heavily on irrigation, diverting scarce surface water and over-extracting groundwater. This water-equity concern — water-guzzling cash crops in water-scarce zones — is a recurring policy debate, not a soil-nitrogen or transport issue.
questions.subject: Geography
